subject: chemistry_2
question_text: What are primary and secondary batteries? Give one example for each.

verification.note: Unit 3 (Electro Chemistry) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.69-72, which prints the question and a model answer. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK SLOPPINESS (book p.70, SAQ 1): the printed secondary-battery answer says the cell "is made to operate in the reserve direction"; the word is REVERSE. It also gives the example only as "storage battery", which names no cell; the lead storage battery is named here. ELECTRODE REACTIONS: the dry cell and lead accumulator reactions added on this card are taken from the book's own LAQ 6 answer (book p.72) and were checked for atom and charge balance. Cathode of the dry cell: MnO₂ + NH₄⁺ + e⁻ → MnO(OH) + NH₃ balances with 1 Mn, 2 O, 4 H, 1 N and zero net charge on each side. Lead accumulator overall: Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O balances with 2 Pb, 2 S, 10 O, 4 H. LONG ANSWER PAIR: LAQ 6 of the same unit asks for the construction and working of each type (card ts_ipe_c2_ec_types_of_batteries); this SAQ is kept to the two definitions and one example each.

steps.label: Primary battery
lines: A primary battery is a galvanic cell in which
the cell reaction happens only once.
When the reactants are used up the cell stops
working and cannot be used again, because its
reaction cannot be reversed by passing current
from an outside source.
steps.why: The dividing line between the two types is whether the cell reaction can be driven backwards. In a primary cell the products move away from the electrode or change form, so passing current the other way does not rebuild the original substances.
common_mistakes: Saying a primary cell is one that is used first. Primary means the reaction cannot be reversed, not that it comes first.
Saying it has no electrolyte. Every cell has an electrolyte; the difference is whether it can be recharged.
steps.memory_tip: Primary means one way only: the reaction runs forward and cannot be driven back.
steps.margin_note: The words cannot be recharged, with the reason, carry this mark. A definition without the reason usually gets half.

steps.label: Example of a primary battery
lines: Example: the dry cell, which is a modified
Leclanche cell.
The emf of a dry cell is about 1.5 V.
The mercury cell is another example.
steps.why: The dry cell cannot be recharged because its electrode reactions cannot be reversed. The ammonia formed at the cathode is taken up as the complex ion [Zn(NH₃)₄]²⁺ and the zinc container itself is used up, so there is nothing left in place to be turned back into the starting materials.
common_mistakes: Giving the lead storage battery as the example. That is a secondary battery and can be recharged.
Writing 2e⁻ in the dry cell cathode reaction. Manganese goes from +4 to +3, so only one electron is taken.
steps.memory_tip: Dry cell: zinc case is the anode, and MnO₂ around the carbon rod is the cathode. 1.5 V.
steps.margin_note: Name the cell and give at least the anode reaction. A bare name is usually half this mark.

steps.label: Secondary battery
lines: A secondary battery is a galvanic cell that
can be recharged.
Passing current from an outside source in the
opposite direction reverses the cell reaction
and rebuilds the original substances, so the
cell can be discharged again.
It is also called a storage cell.
steps.why: Recharging works only when the products stay where they were formed. In a secondary cell the products are solids that stick to the electrodes, so the reverse current can turn them back into the starting materials at the same place.
common_mistakes: Saying a secondary battery stores electricity. It stores chemical energy; the electricity is remade when it discharges.
Writing that it never needs recharging. It does discharge, and is then recharged.
steps.memory_tip: Secondary means two ways: discharge runs the reaction forward, charging drives it back.
steps.margin_note: The word reversible, or the sentence about the outside source, is what earns this mark.

steps.label: Example of a secondary battery
lines: Example: the lead storage battery, used in
cars and inverters.
Left to right on discharge, right to left on
charging.
Each cell gives about 2 V.
The nickel and cadmium cell is another
example.
steps.why: Both electrodes turn into the same solid, PbSO₄, and that solid stays stuck to the plates. Because it does not move away, the charging current can convert it back into Pb at one plate and PbO₂ at the other.
common_mistakes: Writing the equation with a single arrow. The double arrow is what shows the cell can be recharged.
Saying the electrolyte is unchanged. Sulphuric acid is used up on discharge, so the acid gets weaker.
steps.memory_tip: Both plates end up as the same white solid, PbSO₄. That is why charging can undo it.
steps.margin_note: Box the reversible equation and mark which direction is discharge. That is the line an examiner looks for.

insider_note: The mark is for the REASON, not the label. A primary cell cannot be recharged because its reaction cannot be reversed; a secondary cell can, because its products stay on the electrodes. Write the reason beside each name.
